tagline.text: A museum of modern and contemporary Philippine art inside the UP Diliman campus

location.label: Location
location.text: M. Roxas Avenue, UP Campus, Diliman, Quezon City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50~300 (admission and transport included, per person)

children.text: The UP Vargas Museum is a university museum on the Diliman campus. It opened in 1987 on the strength of the artworks and materials donated by Jorge B. Vargas, and it offers a quiet way to see modern and contemporary Philippine art and rotating exhibitions.

The official name of the UP Vargas Museum is the Jorge B. Vargas Museum and Filipiniana Research Center. It stands inside the University of the Philippines (UP) campus in Diliman, Quezon City, on the M. Roxas Avenue side. The museum grew out of the art, books, papers, memorabilia, stamps and coins that Jorge B. Vargas collected and left to the university. Construction began in 1983, and President Corazon Aquino inaugurated the building on
February 22, 1987

The museum is run by the UP Diliman College of Arts and Letters. As a result, it has the calm, scholarly atmosphere typical of a university museum rather than the glitz of a tourist gallery. The collection is widely known for works by leading figures of Philippine art history such as Juan Luna, Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, Victorio Edades and Fernando Amorsolo. Besides the permanent collection, solo shows and special exhibitions by younger artists are held often, so you can see something different each time you visit.
The museum is small, so
1–2 hours

is enough even at a relaxed pace. That makes it easy to pair with the Oblation statue, the Sunken Garden and a stroll around the campus for a half-day outing. Unlike the National Museum in central Manila, it is not crowded with tourists, which means fewer people taking photos and more time to linger in front of each work.

For visitors from Korea, this is a good first step into Philippine art. Explanations are mainly in English, but the labels are short and the exhibitions are small, so nothing feels overwhelming. Even if you are not used to art museums, you can simply pick a few works you like and spend time with them. Exhibition themes often connect to local stories such as Philippine history, the colonial experience, labor and the sea, which also offers clues for understanding Philippine society. These interpretations differ from show to show, so rely on the explanations on site.

blocks.title: Permanent collection of modern and contemporary Philippine art

children.text: The permanent art collection is the heart of the museum. Works by painters whose names come up in Philippine art history, such as Juan Luna, Hidalgo, Edades and Amorsolo, are known to be in the holdings. In October 2024, works by women artists including Nena Saguil and Maria Iglesias were presented in the permanent display. The arrangement changes, so check on arrival which works are on view.

blocks.title: Materials donated by Jorge B. Vargas

children.text: Vargas, for whom the museum is named, was a politician and UP alumnus who left his artworks, books, personal papers, memorabilia, stamps and coins to the university. The belongings one person gathered over a lifetime offer a glimpse of collecting culture and the mood of the era in the 20th-century Philippines. An exhibition on Vargas's life as a collector has been held in the past.

An exhibition called "Objects of Study: The PCGG Artworks Collection," which deals with artworks seized and held by a government agency, has been presented here. It goes beyond simply viewing the works and examines their provenance and history, which makes it interesting for anyone curious about modern Philippine history. Check before your visit whether it has reopened and what its current status is.

blocks.title: Special exhibitions and solo shows by young artists

children.text: Special exhibitions change often in addition to the permanent display. In autumn 2024, Jon Cuyson's solo exhibition "Taong Dagat (People of the Sea)" was on view, and earlier an exhibition for children was held. It is a good way to get a light feel for the currents of contemporary Philippine art.
Guided tours are led by university interns and staff. Free tours were offered during National Arts Month in 2023, and the usual rate was announced as about
per group of up to 10 people. Rates may change, so confirm when you book. If you want to understand the background of the exhibitions, a tour is recommended.

blocks.title: The building and the campus atmosphere

children.text: The museum sits within the green UP Diliman campus, so the walk to it already feels like a stroll. The campus has several museums and galleries, which makes it easy to continue on a route of the university's cultural facilities. For other attractions on the same campus, see the UP Diliman entry.

As the formal name "Filipiniana Research Center" suggests, this is both an exhibition hall and a research institution. It holds books, materials and documents, and is visited by many students and researchers. General visitors who want to consult materials should inquire in advance, so ask the staff first.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Museum visit and a walk around the UP campus

children.text: Arrive at
, when the museum opens. You may be asked to leave your bag with the guard at the entrance, so keep valuables on you. In the morning there are few visitors, so you can see the exhibits in peace.
Buy your ticket at the information desk and ask what is currently on view. A good order is to see the permanent exhibition first and then continue to the special exhibitions.
After the visit, walk around the campus. The Oblation statue and the Sunken Garden are within walking distance. If the weather is hot, the morning or late afternoon in the dry season is recommended.
Have lunch at a restaurant near the campus. Afterward you can head back downtown or look around the shops near the school.
The museum
is closed on Mondays and Sundays
and often on holidays as well, so it is safest to plan your visit for a weekday morning.

items.title: Exhibition-focused route
items.subtitle: Going deeper with a guided tour

children.text: Book a guided tour in advance by email or phone. Groups are asked to notify the museum at least 48 hours ahead.
See the permanent collection and the special exhibitions in order with your guide. Hearing how the works came to be makes even the same painting look different.
When the tour ends, ask whether there is an exhibition catalog or handout. If you are interested in Philippine art, pick up materials on the special exhibitions.
From anywhere in Metro Manila, such as Makati or BGC, first set the UP campus in Diliman, Quezon City as your destination. The museum is on the M. Roxas Avenue side of the campus.
From the airport, taking a taxi or ride-hailing car from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) is easiest. Depending on traffic it can take
over 1 hour
, so avoid rush hours.
Bus and jeepney routes change often, so check current routes on a map app. Jeepneys run toward the UP campus from the Quezon Avenue and Commonwealth side.
Check exact routes and fares locally.
It is easiest to enter "Vargas Museum" or "UP Diliman" in a ride-hailing app such as Grab.
Some roads inside the campus may have traffic restrictions, so you may have to get out at the entrance and walk.
The campus is large, but the main facilities are within walking distance of each other. Bring a hat and water during the hot daytime.
Student jeepneys (Ikot) sometimes run inside the campus, but check the route locally.

The museum is mostly indoors, so it is less affected by the season, but because you walk around the campus it is wise to consider the weather. The most comfortable weather is between November and February.
The museum is open from Tuesday to Saturday. UP community members enter free on Wednesdays, so more students may visit that day. For a quiet visit, the morning is recommended.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: A good time if you want to include a campus walk
Visit the museum in the morning and stick to shade when moving around the campus
Plan around indoor exhibits and bring an umbrella

There is no restaurant inside the museum, so use the restaurants and cafes in and around the UP campus. Around the campus there are many simple restaurants and cafes for students, so you can have a meal cheaply. Check on the day whether they are open.

Rather than staying right next to the museum, many visitors book a hotel elsewhere in Quezon City or in a larger area such as Makati or BGC. The Diliman area is a university district and relatively quiet, but traffic is heavy, so allow plenty of travel time.

If you are not ready to head home after the museum, a cafe near the campus gate is a good place to rest. University-area restaurants get crowded at lunchtime during the school term, so you will wait less if you go before
or after
. Some shops close during school breaks, so check the business information on your map app.
The museum is listed as open Tuesday to Saturday, from
to
. It is often closed on Sundays, Mondays and holidays, so confirm before you go.
On Wednesdays, UP students, staff and alumni get in free by showing a UP ID. This does not apply to general tourists.
The listed contacts are phone (02) 8981-8500 and email vargasmuseum@up.edu.ph. Contact the museum in advance for groups or guided tours.
You can leave large bags at the entrance. Keep valuables and your phone with you.
Do not touch the works in the galleries, and ask the staff first whether photography is allowed.
There is a lot of walking on the campus, so bring comfortable shoes, an umbrella and water.
The campus has several museums and galleries, so events increase during Museums and Galleries Month in October.
The official website is sometimes not available, so get in the habit of checking social media announcements or calling.
Fees and opening hours differ between sources and change often. Confirm directly with the museum just before your visit.
Some galleries may close while exhibitions are being changed.
The museum may close on holidays and during school events.
Campus access rules may change, so follow the guard's instructions at the entrance.
Moving around the campus is hot at midday in summer. Bring water.
Heavy traffic can delay your arrival, so leave some extra time.

This is the main campus of the University of the Philippines, where the museum is located. The Oblation statue and the Sunken Garden are within walking distance, so it pairs well with the museum for a half-day route.
A park about
15–30 minutes
away by car. The time varies with traffic, so check on a map app.
The National Museum of the Philippines is in central Manila. Its character differs from that of a university museum, so it is interesting to compare the two.

blocks.title: Other museums and galleries at UP Diliman

children.text: The campus is said to have nine museums and galleries in all. If you have time, look around them as well.
